utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kindly call the case, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the could the room. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al., thank you Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Monday. Good afternoon to all the people present in the courtroom, to the OTP representatives, to the Defence counsel, the accused, and good afternoon to the registrar and the usher as well. We have two oral rulings. Let's start with the first one. It has to do with the request or motion by the Prosecution asking for a full summary of the testimony by Neven Tomic. On the 6th of October, 2008, the Prosecution filed a motion with the Trial Chamber for Prlic Defence to be asked to supply an adequate summary of the testimony of Neven Tomic pursuant to Rule 65 ter by the 10th of October, 2008 at the latest. On October 9, 2008, the Prlic Defence filed a pleading in which it provided additional information concerning Neven Tomic's testimony. His testimony is scheduled to start on the 27th of October, 2008. After reviewing the Prlic Defence filing, the Trial Chamber is of the view that the Prlic Defence has supplied enough information for the Prosecution to adequately prepare for the cross-examination of Neven Tomic. For instance, the Prlic Defence mentioned parts of the indictment to which the witness will speak, such as Croatisation, ethnic cleansing, and the knowledge that Prlic allegedly had of events that took place in detention centres. The Prlic Defence further submits that Neven Tomic's testimony will deal with other points dealt with by previous witnesses, such as witnesses Puljic, Kozulj, Perkovic, and Primorac. On the basis of the additional information provided by the Prlic Defence, the Trial Chamber dismisses the motion by the Prosecution. Second oral ruling, which is a request for observations from the Prosecution with relation to the expert report provided by the Prlic Defence expert report of Milan Cvikl.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Excuse me, Your Honour. I apologise for interrupting the Chamber, but I'm afraid if I don't, it may be to cause further confusion for everyone. Excuse me. I'm just trying to get sorted here. Your Honour -- good afternoon I should say first of all. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. President, I do apologise interrupting you and I know that's not very polite, but under the situation I feel that before the Chamber proceeds further announcing these rulings, I need to say that I had asked to address the Chamber this afternoon before the witness came in as the registrar will confirm, and I was going to bring to the Chamber's attention some additional developments concerning these very matters, and it appears with to me with the greatest of respect to the Chamber that some of these matters should be brought to the Chamber's attention before the Chamber rules further on these items including the ruling that was just announced. I was reluctant to get to my feet because I didn't want to interrupt the Court, but based on what was filed last Thursday -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm still getting a lost feedback for some reason. Based on the filing that the Prosecution made -- excuse me my apologies. Based on the submission that the defence made on Thursday, the prosecution has continued to look at that and based on some additional information it learned at the end of last week has continued to consider its position. And with great -- with great respect to the Chamber did not expect the Chamber to necessarily address those matters first thing this afternoon. There are very important developments relating to both of these topics that with greatest of respects the Chamber should have in front of it before making a further decision on the one it just made in terms of the Tomic summary and in relation to the expert report. I can -- I can bring those matters to the Chamber's attention now as way of a preview. We are in the process of preparing written submissions that will be filed later this afternoon that touch on both of these matters. And I think -- and again, Your Honour, with the greatest of respect and apologies for interrupting the Chamber these are matters that the Chamber should consider before addressing these matters further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be heard for a second just -- Mr. President. With respect to your ruling on -- on Mr. Tomic, now that we have a ruling, and I didn't believe the Prosecution filed a request to file a reply, it would seem to me that they'd have to seek leave. So I would suspect that -- I would ask for that. And certainly this is the first I hear that there is a problem with the Tomic submission that we filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, concerning Tomic, the Trial Chamber handed down an oral ruling, and as things stand there's no reason to go back on it unless there is a motion for review filed later on. Let me continue what I was reading regarding the expert report. On the 7th of October, 2008, the Prosecution filed a motion for the testimony of experts Milan Cvikl and Svetlana Radovanovic's testimony to be dismissed as there are proposed by the Prlic Defence, the ground being that to date the Prosecution had not received the two expert reports and related documents. The testimony of the said witnesses was initially scheduled to start on the 5th of November and on the 7th of November 2008 respectively. On the 10th of November, 2008, the Prlic Defence filed further to Rule 94 bis the expert report of Milan Cvikl, his CV, and the documents related to his report. On the same day the Prlic Defence disclosed an amended witness schedule indicating that the testimony of Milan Cvikl was postponed until the 17th of November, 2008. The Prlic Defence also indicated that it would like to have four hours for the examination-in-chief of the witness. The Trial Chamber therefore seeks further observations from the Prosecution based on the filing of the expert report and the new date for the testimony of Milan Cvikl. Mr. Scott, you have the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be a minor mistake on line 19, page 4. It's not 10th of November, it's 10th of October. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. President, good afternoon and good afternoon to all those in the courtroom. Once again, Your Honour, I apologise for the unusual interruption of the Chamber in the process of issuing a ruling, and I only did it out of great reluctance but the need -- the felt need to make certain points available to the Chamber. The points are related as to the current witness, the witness who is about to start today, and also relates really implicates three different witnesses at least -- in fact, probably more, but it relates to the current witness, again today's witness, Mr. Zelenika, and I understand there is no request for protective measures. That's why I'm not seeking private session. If I'm wrong, Counsel, please correct me. The issues relate to Mr. Zelenika, Mr. Tomic, and the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... please. I believe the witness mentioned by my learned friend does have protective measures. We haven't heard yet if he has maybe waived them in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: First I've heard of it, Your Honour, and I asked the registry beforehand if there had been any application, and I was told no. So I will pause now to be told -- corrected if I'm wrong. I suppose Mr. Karnavas would know whether he's seeking protective measures for the witness or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He did on a prior occasion -- good afternoon, Your Honours. On a prior occasion the gentleman when he testified before this Tribunal had testified with protective measures. This time he's not seeking protective measures, although we will be going into private session at some point due to some of the testimony and the fear of his life of certain individuals who still remain at large in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which neither the state nor the OTP has done anything about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there's no protective measures in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, then I will proceed in fact in open session. The issues that the Prosecution is raising this afternoon which will be followed by written submissions on these matters. As saying a moment ago, implicates three witnesses; today's witness, Mr. Zelenika; a future witness Mr. Tomic; and the proposed expert Mr. Cvikl. What we have learned in connection with the preparation and submission to the Prosecution for the first time, the Cvikl Report at the it end of last week, is that in the course of preparing his -- conducting his work and preparing his report, Mr. Cvikl has relied extensively on interviews with various Defence witnesses, including Mr. Zelenika, Mr. Tomic, and a past witness, Mr. Akmadzic. Those indicate that those witnesses were interviewed in December of 2007, more than 10 months ago. None of those interviews have been provided to the Prosecution in violation of Rule 67(A) as statements of these witnesses. The -- it is clear that if these statements, these interviews, were important enough to provide to Mr. Cvikl, they are important enough to be provided to the Prosecution. In at least 21 instances, I say at least because we're still in the process of reviewing an extensive set of material that was just put on our -- dropped in our laps last Friday or Thursday night, there are at least 21 references in which Mr. Cvikl says he relied for his point on the evidence of Mr. Zelenika and cites in his footnotes to interviews with Mr. Zelenika in December 2007, more than ten months ago. Those interviews -- that information has not been provided to the Prosecution, and we submit that under Rule 67(A)(i) the Prosecution is entitled to that information and material prior to the cross-examination of this witness. It also Your Honours, as I indicated directly implicates the witness Tomic. Mr. Tomic is cited in the Cvikl report at least 161 times, let me repeat that, 161 times, based on an interview again conducted in -- one or more interviews conducted in December 2007. Those interviews have not been provided to the Prosecution, and it's our submission that no examination of Mr. Tomic, either -- well, either direct but certainly not cross cannot proceed until such time as the Prosecution has been provided with this interview material and had its chance to fully study and prepare for it in connection with cross-examination. I mention in passing that this not only implicates future witnesses, but it implicates past witnesses. Mr. Akmadzic is also cited a number of times in the report again having apparently been interviewed in December of 2007 prior to the time he appeared before the Chamber earlier this year and without any of that information being disclosed or provided to either the Chamber or the Prosecution. So, Your Honour, we think it's in the Prosecution's -- it's the Prosecution's respectful submission that these raise extremely important matters which directly impact all of these items and was going to be part of, and I say part of, an additional submission on the Tomic summary which we have been preparing over the weekend, and that's what I intended and again for which I apologise interrupting the Chamber so that I could make the Chamber aware of that before the Chamber made its ruling. We now also tender -- we will now also be submitting motions concerning the witness Tomic, as I said, the witness Zelenika will be filed later today, and also a further motions and further submissions which in fact the Chamber just requested or just invited concerning the expert. Your Honour, we think these are serious matters that need to be brought to the Chamber's attention. The Prosecution cannot -- cannot and should not be required to cross-examine this witness until all the information required by the rules has been provided to it. This Chamber very specifically in the earlier proceedings this year, I believe it was around -- the deadline was around the 28th of April, if I'm not mistaken, specifically told the Defence to disclose all prior statements and information of this sort of the witnesses. Now, according to Mr. Cvikl report, these interviews existed at least -- at least by December 2007, some months before the Chamber issued its record. It should have been disclosed to the Prosecution on -- in a timely way as required not only by the Rules but as required by the Chamber's scheduling record. We will make written submissions on all of these points, Your Honours, but I bring it to the Chamber's attention with great respect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may briefly respond, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just one moment. Mr. Scott said that he was going to file some submissions. You'll be able to reply. What do you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's not -- he doesn't get to have 30 minutes wave time around television, and then I'm going to be cut off and do it that way, because now he's challenged our integrity and he's led you to leave that there are statements. The gentleman could have just picked up the phone and asked for statements and he would have learned the following: First and foremost, I have no statements. I didn't take the statements. I didn't meet with these particular individuals when Mr. Cvikl met with them. Secondly, as I understand, and if the gentleman had read the report, perhaps he hasn't, but if he had read it carefully, Mr. Cvikl went on a field trip and met with certain individuals, and he had a conversation. I have not been provided with the contents of those conversations. I saw them in the footnotes just like he has. So he's no more at a disadvantage than I am. Thirdly, if he wanted to -- more details on what happened, perhaps we could ask the gentleman, Mr. Cvikl, and he can elucidate as to what, if anything, he has learned. I can assure the trial chamber that I did ask if the gentleman had any handwritten notes knowing full well I would get this sort of response if I dare not turn up any notes the gentleman might have had, and I was told that he didn't keep the notes. That's what I'm told. That's the information that I have, so I am at a disadvantage as Mr. Scott is. I do take exception to sort of the innuendo that we have violated orders and we are not being ethical and so on and so forth, and I leave that to you, Your Honours to figure out. But as far as I know he had some conversations with respect to what he -- to his mandate, which was we provided him with certain information. We also said if you look at the report, if there's any other additional information that he needs to look at as an expert he should go ahead on his own. In other words, don't do what the Prosecution did with Tomljanovich. Instead, here is what we think. Go out and do more. Don't do what Dr. Ribicic did, the Slovenian, the other Slovenian expert did, with is never talk to anybody, don't update your knowledge on any other material that might be available. Don't even speak to the individuals that might have been in place but instead make assertions such as there was no such thing as municipalities having Official Gazettes and the indication that Mostar, by having one, is one more indication that it is taking on state powers. We wanted to avoid the pitfalls and follies that the Prosecution has shown us throughout the trial. And by the way, this is the same practice that I have done throughout my career, and I've never had a problem. I tell my experts here's the information. Here are the questions we want you to ask. If you think there is any additional information, go for it. If you need to interview anybody, go for it. And unfortunately and with regret, I don't have his notes. I am equally at a disadvantage and I can understand the Prosecution's concerns, but I can assure the Trial Chamber that I have no statements. I was not present during those interviews. I don't know what exactly transpired. I assume he was asking technical questions related to the issues that he was dealing with, which was the economics and the laws that were in place. If you look at the -- what he put together, it was basically -- you see the first part, you know, how did the system work during the Yugoslavian area -- era, and then how it functioned at the state and the municipal level -- or I should say the republican and then the municipal level and then he looked at more specifically Mostar and other municipalities, because by and large what we're trying to show is that all this -- these decrees that were passed, what was -- what were the benefits, what were the detriments, what needed to be done with the vacuum created with Sarajevo being under siege. I maintain that we have been fully ethical, and we turned over the report as soon as we were able to, not one second later. So if the Prosecution wishes to file additional submissions after this, that's fine, but I assume next time perhaps he could just pick up the phone and ask, and we would have told him this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you are telling us you have no written documents regarding these interviews and conversations as you have said. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all I'm not going to respond on all the attacks on the Prosecution's practices which of course is always Mr. Karnavas's way. The experts did their work on this -- the Prosecution's experts did their work in a professional matter, the Chamber received their evidence and of course will make the determination of the weight to give to that evidence but I'm not going to get into a tit for tat with Mr. Karnavas with respect to the Prosecution witnesses who have testified to date the Prosecution -- except for this one and this is very important, and that is when the Prosecution -- excuse me when the Chamber contrast the extensive advanced notice given by the Prosecution in every instance of its experts and the minimal, absolutely minimal, and in our view, not even required by the rules has been provided to the prosecution and that will be our continuing submission, our position, and the fact that we received that last week has not changed our position, and the fact that we have one more week will not and has not chained our position. It's not what the Rules require, it's not what this Court's Scheduling Order require. I just ask the Court all of you come in here with your very -- very capable legal minds and common sense. Listen to what Mr. Karnavas is telling us. That an expert, an expert -- someone who holds himself as an expert and knows and knows he's going to be coming into court and defending this material cites a particular witness as the source of his report for the conclusions in his report cites a witness 161 times, and Mr. Tomic -- and Mr. Karnavas stands up and says, But he didn't keep any record of that. No notes, nothing? No record of that? I ask the Chamber to assess that situation and the disadvantage and prejudice done to the Prosecution in this situation. Mr. Karnavas says he's at an equal disadvantage. I'm not sure what that disadvantage is, Your Honour, with great respect. It's not -- he doesn't have to cross-examine this witness, and I'm sure he's happy to tender the report, but the Prosecution, unlike the Defence, has to cross-examine this witness, is entitled to all the material, all the material on which the expert relied in coming to the conclusions that he did, and that is not provided, and I just go back to the nature of the report. When you look at all these footnotes and the 161 footnotes where Mr. Tomic is cited, interview of Neven Tomic, December 2007, and we go to the supporting materials, oh, well, surely the interviews must be attached -- surely the interviews, the source material on which the expert relies certainly must be attached. We go and we open all these materials, the DVDs, and guess what? None of the interviews are there. Nothing. Just a big fat zero, nothing for Tomic, for Zelenika, and all that. So we have an expert who says, "I relied on these people. I relied on these people. I'm going to give that information to the Chamber but the evidence that I based it on is not available to you." It's great prejudice to the Prosecution, Your Honour both as to the expert report and our ability to meet the evidence of these coming witnesses, and that's our position. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let us wait for your submissions. Before the witness comes in, Mr. Karnavas, you gave us the schedule for your witnesses. Thank you for that. We have a better idea until the 27th of November. I added up the number of hours, 24 hours as of today. Does this mean that after the 27th of November, you don't have any more witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: None that are planned, Your Honour and I don't intend to all more witnesses. The remainder of the time we were going to reserve for the other phases, but that's our witness list. We don't anticipate adding anyone. We're not looking into adding anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is indeed how I understood your filing. At any rate, we're waiting for the OTP's submissions with great trepidation, and the Trial Chamber will issue a ruling on the basis of the submissions. We take due note that Mr. Karnavas said that he did not have any report or personal notes or memos from Cvikl following the conversations or interviews he may have had with other witnesses including Mr. Neven Tomic. But Mr. Zelenika is due to come, so -- Zelenika, so the Prosecution can ask them whether Cvikl, when he met with him, took notes, or listened to them orally without taking any notes. That's all we know so far. At any rate, Mr. Karnavas said that he has nothing else in his possession. Back to you, Mr. Karnavas. I put the question to you for a good reason. We know that after you we'll have the Stojic Defence with their witnesses. The Trial Chamber just wants to organise future scheduling. And you do confirm that you will have your last witness on the 27th of November; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Barring an action and/or some sort of a force majeure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, not to try the Chamber's patience, but as long as we're on that additional the matter, again I just want to mention so there's no prejudice to anyone, Defence or Prosecution or the Chamber, there are still of course the outstanding matter of potential Rule 92 bis witnesses, Your Honour, and those motions haven't been filed, and of course, of course the Prosecution may seek cross-examination of those witnesses which presumably would have to be scheduled sometime after the 27th of November. So just so long as the Chamber is aware. And I'm sure the Chamber is, but just as a reminder. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, yes. Do you have -- or how many 92 bis witnesses do you have, because you mentioned this. I can't remember exactly. You mentioned some, not many, but you had some.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There are two categories. The first category are witnesses who have testified before this Tribunal and have been cross-examined by either Mr. Scott, Mr. Stringer, or others in previous cases, and so if they want to call those witnesses back to take another shot at the cross-examination, you know, that's up to them. Then there will be three or four other statements there about a page to a page and a half, and as I've indicated, I believe I must have indicated this to the Prosecutor, maybe I did it verbally, but by and large these witnesses are sort of -- they would fall into the category of character witnesses. They are post -- post-Washington period and so that's what these witnesses are, and of course the Prosecution is free to call them if they wish to call them, but as I said, they're one to two pages long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, when will you tell us about these 92 bis, soon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we're add -- as we speak, I'm -- unfortunately you can make requests sometimes months in advance and you're still waiting. I'm hoping that by the end of the week I will have those four small statements I spoke of. As far as the others -- and I must apologise -- I anticipated having that part of the motion in earlier. I can assure the Trial Chamber that I'm going to endeavour to have that by either the end of the week or first part of next week, but again those witnesses have been cross-examined by three members, I believe, of the Prosecution team, and so -- and I don't see the purpose of bringing them in to cross-examine them again on content that they've already been cross-examined on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] Therefore, we will have -- thank you very much for your answers to our request. Yes. I see the beginning of the interpretation is missing. I say you gave us a list of exhibits with chapters as I had requested a week ago, and this will help us to follow your own examination, and this will be very useful. Thank you so much. Please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While the witness is coming back, I want to make sure that one point is made clear, that not only do I not have any notes but never did I ever give any instructions to -- to Mr. Cvikl either not to take notes or to destroy any notes that he might have taken. So I just want to make sure that -- because the implication may be that he's been instructed not to. So that's what I wanted to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Please state your name, your name and your birth date, if you please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mirko Zelenika, 25th August, 1947.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Closed session, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you -- what is your work today? Are you working or not working? And if you are working, could you tell us what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm retired now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Will you please make the -- take the oath and read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. A few brief explanations about this hearing. You know it is going to last four days to hear you. First of all, you will have to answer questions from Mr. Karnavas. You probably met Mr. Karnavas before in order to prepare this hearing. He will ask you questions, and he will show you some documents. At the end of that, the other counsel of the other accused may also question you within the framework of their cross-examination. The Prosecution, who is on your right-hand side, Mr. Scott, will also question you in the framework of cross-examination, and he will have the same question time as Mr. Karnavas. The four Judges you may see may also ask questions from you and maybe, according to the documents shown, or after the cross-examinations or examinations. This will depend. Try and be extremely precise in your answers when you answer the questions, and if you don't understand a question, don't hesitate and ask the person who is questioning you to reformulate. We have a break for 20 minutes every hour and a half, but if during the hearing you don't feel well, raise your hand and we will stop the session so that you may take a rest. You made a solemn declaration to say the truth and the whole truth, so this means that you are now a witness, and you do not -- you're not a witness of one or the other party. You don't have any contact any more with either Mr. Karnavas nor Mr. Prlic. This is what I wanted to tell you. Of course if at any time you wish to ask a question from the members of the Chamber, don't hesitate to ask us. Raise your hand then. We are at your entire disposal. This is what I wanted to tell you as an introduction, and I will now give the floor to Mr. Karnavas, who shall now start the -- his examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, good afternoon, Mr. Zelenika.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First, I'm going to begin by asking you some basic questions about your background. If you could tell us where you're from and the level of your educations.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: My name is Mirko Zelenika, born to gather Ivan and mother Milka born on the 25th of August, 1947, in a place called Risovac, Jablanica municipality, the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I got a degree in political science, majoring in social policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please describe to us up until 1991 the types of positions that you've held, the kind of work that you did up until 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: In my career, from 1967 I worked for a year and a half as a teacher, then another 18 months as a secretary in a primary school. Then I worked in a socially owned business, the Granit Company as a clerk dealing with affairs of social standard. Then I supervised a section for human resources and general affairs. Then from 1984 to 1986 I was the president of the Executive Council of Jablanica municipality, which means the head of the local government, after which I returned to the Granit Company where I was a manager of the unit for joint services. And just before 1991 I was on standby waiting for my permanent employment to resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zelenika. Now, as I understand it, at some point in time, and you can tell us exactly when, you became again the President of the Executive Board or Executive Council in the Jablanica municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What were the dates?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: It was the 11th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how long did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: For about six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before we speak about that period, if you could briefly -- I'll -- let me just ask one quick question and then we'll going into more details. When you compare the way the Executive Council operated in 1991 for the six months that you were there and look back to when you were the president of the Executive Council in 1984 to 1986, did it function -- the rules of procedure and how it functioned, was it the same or was it different?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The rules of procedure that applied when I was president of the executive down in 1992 were the same as in the period 1984 to 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So let's talk a little bit about your experience in 1984 and 1986 and we're only interested in knowing somehow this board, how this Executive Board functioned and, in particular, your position as president, how you fit within the board. So would you please tell us a little bit about that. How did the Executive Board fit into this?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: It was a collective body of executive local power consisting of some members who were heading local secretariats, municipal secretariats, and some outside members, renowned businessmen with extensive experience nominated by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, as President of the Executive Board were you above everyone else with, for instance, extra powers for voting or being capable of making decisions and issuing orders, making appointments without consultation, or were you just one -- one member with equal rights, that is, one vote?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I was actually one of the members with one vote, and I had no powers outside the sessions of the Executive Council to appoint or promote anybody or anyone -- anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, when decisions were made and when appointments made, who signed those decisions or appointments on behalf of the Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: When decisions were made on appointments or any other decisions, after the decision-making process I signed such decisions, among others, as the president of the Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So those decisions or appointments were not yours but, rather, they were taken by the collective body.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you would have to sign a decision or appointment even if you had voted against it but it had passed because of the majority of voting?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. My vote was just one among the total number of votes in the Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's fast forward a little bit to 1991, 1992. First let me ask you whether you were a member of a political party at the time. This is leading up to the elections, the first free elections.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I was not affiliated to any political party before the democratic elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you were ultimately re-appointed to the position of President of the Executive Board or Council in 1992, could you please tell us how is it that you got that appointment?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Already earlier in 1991 the elected president of the Executive Council was recalled, and in Jablanica we were facing the declaration of the immediate threat of war and thus the Assembly of the municipality was not functioning any more. There was in its place an operative body called the Crisis Staff. That Crisis Staff of Jablanica municipality appointed me on the 11th of May to be the next president of the Executive Council of Jablanica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, had you ban member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, had you been associated with or involved in any of the secretariats of the Crisis Staff or the Executive Board prior to your appointment, that is, as President of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning of 1992 -- sorry, 1991, I was elected secretary of the secretariat for the economy, social affairs and general management, and I was thus president of the Executive Council of Jablanica municipality from 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. You were -- you were a member of the Executive Council since 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- and that was by virtue of your position?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And when you say "secretariat," that's similar to a department; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: You could put it that way, although within the framework of the secretariat they are -- there are lower organisational units that are called departments and sections, but you could put it that way. It's one of the bodies of municipal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. When you say that you were elected, how were you elected to the secretariat position, or were you actually appointed or nominated and, if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I was appointed, therefore not elected, pursuant to the electoral results of various political parties at the elections in Jablanica in 1990. I was nominated by the Croatian Democratic Union to the position of secretary of the secretariat that I mentioned before, and on that basis, I was nominated into the Executive Council of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at that time when you were nominated by the HDZ, were you a member of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I was not a member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if I understood your earlier answer, based on the electoral results, the parties were allocated certain positions within the political structure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we fast forward to the -- to the time when you were appointed as president of the Executive Council, were -- who nominated you for that position? Was it political party or was it a body?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: In 1992. We're talking about 1992. There was a Crisis Staff in operation, and based on an internal agreement between several political parties, I was nominated into the Executive Council as president. So it was not just the nomination from the HDZ. It was an agreement between the political parties that were active in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just so we have a clear understanding, what were the political parties at the time that were members of the Crisis Staff or their representatives? How many political parties were representative, I should say, in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: All political parties that existed at the time. If you want me to enumerate them I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that was the purpose of my question. If you can help me out here. We know the SDA and the HDZ. We've covered those. The SDP would have been one of the others.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: SDP, but also the Liberal Party. I can't remember any more. Some youth party, perhaps. There were at least five of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And based on the electoral results, were you entitled to hold such a high position since you were -- initially you came into the Crisis Staff -- or you initially came into the -- the secretariat by virtue of the appointment by HDZ. Was the HDZ in a position of having someone hold that high a position, that is president of the Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Excuse me. Your Honour, I'm trying to be minimal in the objections I make, but there's been substantial leading questions being put to the witness from the very beginning, and I have deferred to it or not raised the issue until now, but if these are important enough questions for Mr. Karnavas to put to the witness and he apparently thinks they are, then they shouldn't be leading in nature. Just put open-ended questions, and let's receive the evidence of the witness and not the evidence of Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't aware that leading was of such nature. I should also point out that the gentleman did provide the OTP with an extensive 92 bis statement that they used in another case. So this is not new information to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. That has nothing to do with whether it's leading or not. The question is leading no matter what disclosure I have. It's leading, and we object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Based on -- yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have the impression there were any leading questions. Those are questions which are extremely complex, and in order to try and understand something in all this the questions have to enable us by their answers to sort this out. Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you were elected to -- as president of the Executive Council, how was that received by the members?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: My name had been put forward by all the parties pursuant to their agreement, and there was a general consensus on this. I had not -- my name had not been put forward bit HDZ alone, because the HDZ had not gotten a result at the election that would have guaranteed the party that sort of role in the local government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, were you actually formally appointed to the position? Was your position certified, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No. The Crisis Staff, based on certain regulations, had the power to pass certain enactments, orders, decisions, conclusions, but whatever the Crisis Staff passed, when needed they had to submit to the Assembly for the Assembly to ratify all of that. Therefore, the certification or ratification of my appointment never happened at any of the Assembly meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Was the Assembly still meeting on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: On and off. No more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how long did the Crisis Staff -- how long was it in existence, until what period?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the Crisis Staff existed from May on for at least two months, after which it was renamed and was now called the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you tell us whether there were any changes, now that it went from Crisis Staff to the War Presidency? Did its membership in any way change, and whether its functions changed in any way, could you please tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: This should be simple enough for me to explain. The only change occurred to the name. As far as the powers of that body were concerned in terms of decision making, there were no changes. The War Presidency continued to do the same thing that the Crisis Staff had been doing previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's talk about that a little bit. Just very briefly, if you could tell us what sorts of things was the War Presidency doing? What was it competent of doing, and what was it in fact doing?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The War Presidency had all the powers that under the law, under the constitution, and under the municipality's statute were envisaged in relation to the Assembly as a body of delegates. Nevertheless, the Presidency was an operative body, the scope of whose work was much narrower. In addition to the standard issues discussed by the Assembly, the Presidency under its statute and under the law had the power to analyse and monitor emergency situations such as the one we were now facing across Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was an immediate threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, during that time when you had the Crisis Staff and then later on the War Presidency, were there any armed forces in and around Jablanica municipality and, if so, could you please tell us what those forces were?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Well, the Crisis Staff was in existence -- while the Crisis Staff was in existence and now that there was the War Presidency, there were some armed forces around. The Territorial Defence on the one hand, the Green Berets, the Patriotic League united under the name of Territorial Defence for a while and then at different time known as the armed forces. On the other hand there was the armed component element of the Croatian Defence Council, and these were two armed components or forces that had equal rights in every way, their shared objective being to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And based on that answer I take it the HVO was accepted as a legitimate component of the armed forces of Jablanica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just to be consistent, that's a leading question. That is exactly a leading question. He took -- Mr. Karnavas told him the answer he was looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, it is Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond. If you look at the previous answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will respond, Mr. Karnavas, but I'm looking at the question. You are saying that the HVO was the legitimate armed component in Jablanica. This is a statement you make. That cannot be challenged, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, if you look at the previous answer that the gentleman gave, I mean, I'm -- fine. But if you look at his answer, what has he said? I merely rephrased it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I don't think this is a matter for argument. This is clearly a leading question and please reformulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for that instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What were the legitimate armed forces on the ground in Jablanica municipality at that point?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Am I expected to answer this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I have said this, haven't I? I'm just to repeat. I said that at the time in Jablanica there were two equal and legitimate defence components, one being Territorial Defence, Green Berets and Patriotic League, and this went under the name armed forces and then the other hand there was the Croatian Defence Council and those two components were equal and legitimate. I'm talking about Jablanica municipality, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about these two legitimate armed forces. You said that they were equally recognised. What about the financing of them? Where were they being financed?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The armed forces, Territorial Defence, the Patriotic League, the Green Berets were for the most part bankrolled by the local economy the money generated in Jablanica municipality. The Croatian Defence Council, as far as the military component was concerned, equipment, supplies and so on and so on, from the Main Staff. There had been an agreement that in proportion to their numbers both should be bankrolled to some extent from the budget of Jablanica municipality, 80 per cent in favour of the Muslim armed forces and 20 per cent in favour of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And was that happening, at least to your knowledge, while you were there, 80 to 20 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Well, not for the most part. Not for the most part. And I, as the representative of the Executive Board, would learn about this at meetings of the Crisis Staff or the War Presidency whenever whoever was of charge reported this, saying that they were facing some difficulties making sure the 20 per cent earmarked for the Croatian Defence Council were available at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was there a HVO civilian component operating in and around Jablanica municipality and, if so, can you please describe it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Could you please specify the time-frame in 1992 that you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, when the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency and, of course, keeping in mind that you've already told us about the HVO military component being a legitimate force as one of the legitimate components in Jablanica, was there a civilian HVO in existence at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The military component of the HVO was established sometime earlier on in 1992. It wasn't before much later that the civilian component was set up as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you could please describe to the Trial Chamber what exactly was the civilian component. Describe to it what it amounted to.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The civilian component of the Croatia in Jablanica municipality was a form of self-help or help, if you like, to the Croats in the area. It was also an attempt to assist in a logistical way the military component of the HVO, but it also represented an effort on the part of the entire population throughout Jablanica municipality regardless of their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Was it -- I'm being pointed out to the transcript. It says here component of the November. Do it know where that's coming from. It was an attempt to assist in the logistical way the military component of the what? The HVO military; is that what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, the military component of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did the HVO civilian component ever set up a parallel government in Jablanica municipality, and by that what I mean provided -- you know, have administrative services and establish police with police officers running around with guns and billy clubs and a car, collecting taxes, establishing schools, any of that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Certainly not. This was an advisory body, and that did not include this type of activity or any form of administration at all. There were several persons who were involved who would hold meetings occasionally, and depending on what the situation was that prevailed at a given time they would make the proposals or would advise but they certainly didn't have the authority to exercise power in any of the segments of local life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did it have an office?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: For a while there was no office. Therefore, one might assume what this was all about. You can't have a body of power exercising its function from a tree branch or somewhere out in the street, although there was an office at a later point but it was just to keep them from meeting in private homes, flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, that's what I want to get to. At some point did it have an office and, if so, where was that office located?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: An office was approved by the War Presidency for the HVO. At one point in time it was on the way out of Jablanica town along the road to Sarajevo near the bridge, the hydroelectric power plant. Later on it was in the centre itself of Jablanica town. The street was called Zeljeznicka Street, no number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. When it moved to the centre of the town, who provided those facilities? Did they buy it? Did they rent it? Was it made available and if so, please describe.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Sir, as I pointed out before, even the first offices that was used it was actually a single office and the same applies to the ones later on at Zeljeznicka Street. There were two or three rooms there. That was something that the War Presidency of the Jablanica municipality allowed the HVO to use. It wasn't about renting. This was a socially owned property and the War Presidency had the power to award the use of this office or these rooms in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What about the HVO, the military component? Did they have -- were they located in any particular area? Did they have headquarters, barracks and if, so, where were they located and who provided those facilities?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The military component of the HVO had a room that it was using, and it was using this room jointly with the civilian component, and this is something that was awarded to them by the War Presidency of Jablanica municipality. And then the office moved to Zeljeznicka Street while the military office remained over there in this one room, and this was something that was given to them or granted to them again by the War Presidency of Jablanica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we've had quite a bit of testimony or controversy, whichever you want to call it, concerning territory and area, so let me be very concrete. Did the HVO or the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna carve out any area or territory, whatever you want to call it, within the Jablanica municipality and declare it to be Croatian or belonging to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or the HVO or to the Croat nation, any of the above?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were there ever any attempts by the HVO civilian component, perhaps in conjunction with the military component, to take over the War Presidency, to take over any of the institutions in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were any discussions ever held regarding the HVO or the Croatian Community somehow being involved or associated with or connected to the Jablanica municipality and, if so, please describe.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Certainly not. Despite you being so adamant, I have to answer no. I have no choice but to answer no to all these questions because there was nothing like that at all going on. That simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you yourself, however, ever, when you were either in -- a member of the Crisis Staff or president of the Executive Council ever or thereafter ever bring up the possibility of HZ -- HZ HB, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna being involved or -- let me rephrase it, the Jablanica municipality or the Presidency looking at or being connected to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: There were talks on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And could you please tell us what those talks were about, how far the talks went, what was the purpose, some details?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The talks were about checking if there were any better options to organise life in Jablanica. As time went by, Jablanica was becoming more and more of a dead end. We did know, however, that in some other areas life was organised in a much better way for citizens and for Defence purposes alike and so on and so forth. Therefore, we talked in order to see if we could improve the living conditions, both for citizens and for defence purposes. I must especially point out the fact that at the time Jablanica municipality and especially its main town, Jablanica town, were under pressure, pressure from refugees flooding in. At one point in time there were more refugees living there than the domicile population, the local population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we'll talk a little bit more about that, but since you spoke of the refugees and of the times, were the residents of the Jablanica municipality ever mobilised and, if so, do you recall when?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. More than once. Sometimes there -- there was partial mobilisation and sometimes full mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when we speak of mobilisation, what are we speaking of?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: As far as I understand the term, mobilisation has a number of different aspects. Mobilising military conscripts on the one hand, and then there's also mobilisation in terms of war assignment or civilian protection, and all three were happening depending on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, were you ever mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please describe to us in what fashion?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: As of mid-April 1993, I received a summons for mobilisation into what was termed the work platoon. I was told to report at 7.00 in the morning outside the Jablanica municipality building. I was told to bring along a shovel, a pike, and a saw. The summons also said that should I fail to respond to the call-up, I would be duly prosecuted. I did not respond to the call-up, because I had in my possession a document dating 20 years before, from 1973, when the military medical commission had declared me to be only fit in a very limited form to serve in the armed forces, and document said explicitly that I was unable to stand, walk, march, or stand guard for any extensive period of time. Based on this assessment by the military medical commission, the secretariat for All People's Defence back in 1973 adopted a decision stating that I was unfit for this type of military service as I have now specified. Therefore, my assignment was to the ranks of the civilian protection. I invoked this decision that was then 20 years old, and I failed to respond to the mobilisation call-up. The people from the municipality who had issued the summons sent the police for me. I was taken in by force and brought to the municipality building. I spoke to the secretary who had dispatched my call-up, and I showed him my document. He said he had one of those too dated 20 years ago, and he said it was worthless. He said that all those decisions and medical certificates would now be subject to revision, but until such time it was my duty to report to the call-up, the mobilisation call-up. They called it mobilisation, and I choose to call it forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Were you ever given the opportunity to be medically examined to see whether your condition had changed, you know, whether you were somewhat confabulating or malingering in any way?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you were actually physically examined by a physician?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, did you ask to be examined?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, why weren't you examined?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: When I was summoned by the medical commission, I brought a lot of documents with me because this was a very peculiar illness or condition which I had been suffering from ever since 1961. I had a lot of medical documents about that, and I submitted these documents to the chairman of that medical commission who said he did not have the time to go through those. So he didn't check the documents, and he most certainly didn't check me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what sort of labour -- you said forced labour. Could you just in one minute tell us what sort of forced labour or labour you were asked to -- to do given your condition?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: It was about cutting timber for the purpose of fortifying BH army positions. This was about carrying food, water, and weapons to BH army positions. This was also about other types of manual labour that we were being forced to perform by those who took us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how long did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: From the 15th of April, 1993, to the 8th of September. That's when I was taken prisoner and taken to a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how were you treated in the camp? You don't have to go into all the details at this point, but how were you treated in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: In the shortest possible terms, this was inhumane and cruel treatment in every way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how long were you in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I was in the camp from the 8th of September, 1993, to the 1st of March, 1994, when through the intercession of the International Red Cross I was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who was the war -- who was the president of the War Presidency at the time for the Jablanica municipality, that is, when you were both doing forced labour and then when you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: At the time when I was performing forced labour and when I was in the camp, the president of the Jablanica municipality was Dr. Safet Cibo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you know when Dr. Safet Cibo would have known about you being forced to do labour in light of your medical condition and whether -- and the conditions under which you were in that camp for all those months, or is it possible that he simply didn't know?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I believe he knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. At this point we can take our break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenika, we're going to go to the documents now and you have your folder in front of you, and as I've indicated to you in the past, the documents would be sort of in the order in which I'm going to present them to you. So the first set of documents deal with minutes of meetings that -- that you either attended or are familiar with. So if we could look at first P 00272. That should be your very first document. Do you have it in front of you Mr. Zelenika?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you've had an opportunity to look at this document before coming here today?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We note that it's 19 June, 1992, and we see that your name is under "Others." Is there a particular reason why you're under "Others"?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: It was usual and customary at the sessions of the Assembly to first write the names of members of the council, of the deputies, and then of others. I, as a member of the council, was indicated among "Others."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you a member of the Executive Council at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- and I see that your name comes up here on a couple of occasions. First, can you please tell us what's going on with respect to the discussion concerning your position as chairman of the Executive Committee? We see that on page 4, for instance, there's some indication. If you could just tell us from what you remember.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I can. This was actually the first session of the Municipal Assembly of Jablanica from the day when the Crisis Staff of the municipality nominated me to be the president of the Executive Board, and this was the first opportunity for the Municipal Assembly to verify all the enactments and decisions, conclusions, et cetera that the Crisis Staff had in the period between the two sessions adopted. Among these decisions was the decision to appoint me president of the Executive Board, and this was the first opportunity to confirm that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And was there some sort of an agreement as far as your confirmation went, or was there disagreement? If you could help us out here.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: In the course of the debate and deliberations, I noticed that there was no agreement to confirm my appointment and it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, was that because you were a Croat or a member of HDZ, or was it some other reason?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I understood the reason lay in the fact that the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA, believed that on the basis of the electoral results in 1990 the HDZ should not get the position of the president of the Executive Board, and that was the reason for their reservations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could go to the very last page, at least in English it's page 8, and I direct -- it would be 6 in yours. And I want to direct your attention to "Ivan Rogic," and I understand -- you know who Mr. Rogic is; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If you could look at that segment very briefly, because here Mr. Rogic says they informed the deputies that the decision to build the Jablanica-Posusje road was not being implemented, although work should be completed before next autumn. And then it goes on if we skip one, one sentence, it says: "After hearing the proposals set out by Hamdo Sefer, the Assembly decided that Nijaz Ivkovic and Hamdo Sefer. Would go to Grude as soon as possible so as to work -- so as that work could begin on construction of the Sovici-Risovac section of the Jablanica-Posusje road." Having been there at that meeting, could you please explain to us why were they planning to go to Grude? What was there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I think I can explain that. The thing is that the building of that road was a great challenge in terms of the construction work required. It surpassed our local capacities in Jablanica. And since communication was no longer possible on the thoroughfare towards Mostar, all the traffic from Sarajevo and from Prozor went along the macadam road. That's the reason why help was required from outside, from other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe -- I thought I heard you say that the road to Sarajevo was not possible, or did I mishear you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I said the road from Sarajevo to Mostar was cut off, and traffic was redirected towards the macadam road, Jablanica, Doljani, Posusje, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did that road have a name at some point? Was it given some sort of a name?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. That road was classified as a regional road and had the name R-419. That's an internal name given to it by the maintenance people, whereas we in Jablanica called it the Road of Rescue or the Road of Salvation because that was the only road available from Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But why was Hamdo Sefer or Nijaz Ivkovic, and I assume they're Muslim, why not go to Zenica? Why not go to Tuzla? Why not go to Sarajevo? Why not go some place else? Why are they going to Grude? What's in Grude?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Right. What you're saying is true. Hamdo Sefer and Mr. Nijaz Ivkovic were Muslims, but this kind of assistance and any other kind of assistance was not available from Sarajevo because Sarajevo was absolutely besieged. Had been besieged for a long time before the moment we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But what's in Grude? Why go to Grude? Because there's -- we've heard testimony here that as of 1991, there's a joint criminal enterprise. Now we're seeing there's a meeting here in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. I object to this long commentary. I have no idea why we need to talk about a joint criminal enterprise with a witness as to why go to Grude. We don't need that. If the witness doesn't know, he doesn't have the answer, we can move on. But Mr. Karnavas is coaching the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Nobody's coaching anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, ask him why he wants to go to Grude without talking about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why -- why are these members of this particular meeting, why are they going to Grude? Who's at Grude?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Here is the answer: If we're talking about the road, I know that even before the war there was a specialised company in Grude called Grude Roads which built and maintained roads. So they had the resources required, and the idea was to see if they could help build this road more quickly and maintain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, there's discussion here, and you raise -- you raise the issue with respect to the war budget. Who is going to pay this construction company to come to Jablanica or wherever to build this road? Where was the money going to come from?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: At that time we didn't have any money. We didn't have any money, but we knew that there was money in the region. So that was one reason why we wanted to look into that possibility. But it was possible for us to pay in kind, and we did that. We paid in granite, we paid in timber available in the Jablanica area. So we did not have funds but we had other resources with which to pay in kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, P 0045 -- 546, and this is dated 6 October 1992. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we again see that your name is here, and we see you as a member of the -- present as a member of the Presidency. Can you confirm to us that at this point in time you were indeed a member of the Presidency in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that by that time I was already president, and I was member of the War Presidency at the time we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall being at this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to draw your attention. It would be on page 7 in the English. This would be comments that were made by Salko Zarem, where Mr. -- did you know a Mr. Zarem?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, you are talking about Mr. Zerem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Zerem?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: He was commander of the Muslim armed forces in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I see his name that he is under -- listed as a member of the Presidency if we go to the very first page. So was he a member of the War Presidency at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now here I'm going to read what he says and I'm going to ask you whether you could help us out here. It states here that he says the state of BiH had joined forces consisting of the army of BiH and the HVO and without a mutual cooperation between these components, the whole thing would be difficult. "It is necessary to say that the Muslims were neither organised nor ready at the beginning to fight against the aggressor, and for that reason, they're also very grateful to the Croatian nation for their timely engagement and brave fight against the aggressor." Now, my question is do you recall hearing this gentleman making these comments at this meeting of the War Presidency on 6 October 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to page 10 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, just a technical correction nothing major, but just for the transcript, when the witness was reading from the document -- or it may have been Mr. Karnavas, I'm not sure -- but it came across in line -- let me find it again. On page 45, line 10 it was transcribed as the state of BiH had joined forces. And what the document says is that had joint, j-o-i-n-t, had joint forces and there may be -- there may be a significant difference in that. Just to correct for the record. It's "had joint forces." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go on to -- to page 10 at the beginning of the page in English. This is a comment by Zeljko Siljeg, and he's saying here that: "The HVO introduced check-points and documents in order to protect goods from smugglers and war profiteers, while clearance -- clearances (permissions) were introduced due to the apparent large number of deserters from Bosnia." Can you comment on this observation that is being made by Mr. Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I can by saying that check-points existed both on the side of the Bosnian Muslim armed forces and on the side of the HVO for the same reasons, absolutely the same reasons, and in most cases the people manning those check-points were of mixed ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to the very last page, on page 11, and focusing on what Mr. Matan Zaric indicated, and of course when one reads this document you have to go to page 2 of the English as well, but here he says: "Matan Zaric pointed out again that the companies from Jablanica municipality provided a financial support to the BiH OS and that the Jablanica HVO requires 20 per cent of that support (food, money, and uniforms). The Presidency made right decisions on that, but they are not implemented in reality." Do you see that part?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. First question is: BiH OS, what does that mean? What does OS mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: That means armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who were the armed forces at the time of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Jablanica municipality as is being referred to as BiH OS?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Let me say this again: The armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina were the Territorial Defence, the Patriotic League, and the Green Berets. They had a common name, the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, what is Mr. Matan Zaric saying here about the 20 per cent that was required, food, money, and uniforms, and that the Presidency had made a decision but it wasn't being implemented? What does he mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: He was trying to say that that particular decision was not being honoured and that the 20 per cent of support were not being given to the HVO as an equal, fully fledged and recognised component of the armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next document P 00624. And this is minutes from a session of the 22nd of October, 1992, and now we see your name under "Others -- Other Present." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why are you under "Other" and not above?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
