utterances.text: Because this was a session of the Municipal Assembly, as I explained before on one occasion. The first to be listed were members of parties, deputies, and then others. I belonged with the others, and this listing is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at item 2 on the agenda, and that would be on page 6, and we already -- you introduced us to Salko Zerem, and if we look at the third paragraph of what he's saying, he says here: "The OS," the armed forces, that is, "and the HVO in the territory of the municipality of Jablanica are behaving in accord with the said order of the Supreme Command and the Presidency of BiH. There must be no obstacles in executing the joint logistics support, check-points, joint police, et cetera, although there are some influences from outside slowing it down." Do you see that part?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, can you confirm whether Zerem said those words at that meeting? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I can confirm that. Mr. Zerem said this not for the first time. He had said it before on many other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because at the very last paragraph on page 6, and he says: "If we wish to create a better environment for a more successful defence of the municipality, more contacts and cooperation between the OS and the HVO are needed, there should be barracks with trained soldiers in Jablanica, and we need more support from the Municipal Assembly in general." Can you confirm that he said that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At this point in time, can you please tell us what the environment was in Jablanica? What were the dynamics?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: We're talking now about the period at the end of November 1992. The environment around Jablanica was not really good. There were a series of consequences that had repercussions on Jablanica. There were refugees in Jablanica who, according to information available to me, were larger in number than the local population. I could say that almost 100 per cent of the refugees were Muslim. Many had been traumatized by their past recent experiences and were forced to leave their homes and come to Jablanica. Of course they could not contain sometimes their frustrations and suffering and sometimes the local population got the worse end of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I see in the transcript here on page 49 line 4 that it says at the end of November 1992. Did you mean November or October? Which month are we speaking of?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: It's October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: While we're at this point on lines 5 and 6, it says there were a series of consequences that had repercussions on Jablanica. Should it not be occurrences or events that had repercussions. That consequences have repercussions seems a bit redundant. It doesn't make much sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you concretely, Mr. Zelenika. Other than what you described to us, what were you trying to convey?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I was trying to say that Jablanica was facing a problem, how to ensure that the adverse events in its environment not be reflected in the locality. All these refugees and the armed forces in the municipality had a certain impact, and the problem was how to make sure that this does not engulf us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies, in fact, the issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at page 10 in the English version, we see that you speak. At some point you spoke at this meeting. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And here it says that you presented the councilmen with a chronological overview of difficulties in this composition of Executive Board encompasses the beginning of its work to date. And then later on you say due to the continual harassment, it says you offered to file your resignation or to put your activities on hold until such an agreement had been reached. What exactly were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that. I did inform the councilmen as I had at another session four years earlier of the difficulties that had only grown since then. Namely, it was absolutely impossible to lead that Executive Board any longer knowing that I'm not enjoying the support of all the members of the assembly, and that's why I informed them in so many words that I'm facing an impossible situation. I was unable to pass almost a single decision through the council no matter how good the decision was, as I had meant to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was that because you had difficulties or differences with the other political parties, or had the situation changed in a different direction now?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No, in fact, I didn't have difficulties with the political parties. It was on a personal level. The people who were sitting on the Executive Board, those secretaries of secretariats, were now voting motivated by their ethnicity, not motivated by the quality of the specific proposal. In the whole complement of that local government there were two of us Croats and five Muslims, and I was not able to ensure the enactment of any decision whatsoever. I think that's clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now we can go on to the next document, P 00945. This is 22 December 1992. If we could look at those who are present, we don't see your name; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We do see that Mr. Rogic and Mr. Zaric, which I -- who are Croats, as I understand, were absent; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I just want to focus your attention on just one aspect of -- of this meeting. At some -- at the very first item, we can see that it appears that the Christmas celebration will not take place essentially because of the -- of a curfew. And we see that Father Bosnjak has similar views. Can you please explain what was happening and whether, in fact, there was Christmas mass on Christmas Eve, midnight mass as it normally is held for the Catholics?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. I did not attend this meeting. I had been replaced on the 29th of October, 1992, by a decision of the War Presidency. Nevertheless, as person still living in Jablanica, which is really a small town, I knew about these developments that you address. An explosive device was launched at the local Catholic church in Jablanica causing some material damage. However, the greater damage was the fact that it caused concern among people in Jablanica, especially the Catholics, especially when they found out that the Christmas mass would not be celebrated. For any Catholic the Christmas mass and Christmas itself is one of the most important religious festivities that they mark every year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you told us that you had -- you were no longer on the Presidency. I want to walk you back a little bit and ask you when you were still a member of the Presidency, do you ever recall attending a meeting where Izetbegovic was present and, if so, can you please tell us where and when, and then we'll go into details.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I can remember. This was sometime in the autumn months of 1992. I was called to a meeting being held at the hydroelectric plant in Jablanica having been informed that Mr. Izetbegovic, too, would be attending that meeting. The municipal leaders were there, the party leaders were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. I apologise to the witness. Mr. Zelenika I apologise to you. Your Honours, if terms of -- I was just looking at the summary and I don't see anything in the summary anything about the hydroelectric plant or any meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic. There's no notice of this evidence at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I understand it, Your Honour, first of all the Prosecutor indicated that he wanted no more information. That's first and foremost. Secondly, as I indicated, the gentleman was questioned extensively and extensively by the Prosecution when he gave a 92 bis statement. Obviously either they failed to record it or maybe they failed to ask him all the necessary questions at the time. This information came to my attention today, and so I'm entitled to ask the question and then if you wish to strike it from the record, you could do so but I intend to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: None of those you aren't again we're in a situation neither of Mr. Karnavas's points are responsive to the point. The Prosecution has made no secret of the fact and I'm sure the Chamber is perhaps even tired of hearing, but, unfortunately, we're in a position where we have to keep raising it, the importance of these summaries. It is the only notice, is the only notice of this evidence that we're getting. We don't get statements, and we had the issue earlier today about whether statements should be provided or not, and when we say we're not asking for any additional information, we're saying that we understand then, we understand that the scope of the evidence presented by the witness will be as represented in the summary that we're provided. Now, this is the summary that the Chamber ordered to be provided on 31st of March, 2008. There is nothing in the summary about this topic or subject note. This meeting, a meeting with Izetbegovic, we are caught totally, you know, with no notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, were did you fail to mention in the summary that the witness was planning to mention this meeting with Izetbegovic because he's an important character? Did you think it was secondary at the time, and do you want to change your mind now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I met with the gentleman from Thursday for a couple hours, Friday, Saturday, Sunday, and then today again all the way until 12.30. We went over -- well over 150 documents with the gentleman. During the course sometime today, he had indicated a meeting -- that he recalls a meeting where Izetbegovic was present. We finish the prepping session approximately 12.30, just enough time to reorganize the binders in a particular fashion, provide you with what you've -- what you've indicated, but again it is within the context of when he served as a member of the Presidency. Now, we've heard testimony or there have been some documents that Mr. Izetbegovic had been in Mostar prior -- sometime around this period of time. In fact, I believe that there was a document indicating or reflecting a picture where Izetbegovic had met with my client, Dr. Jadranko Prlic. What is telling about this particular meeting that we learned today that after leaving Mostar Izetbegovic then goes unknowing that he's having --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm entitled to make my record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not in front of the witness. Excuse me. The Prosecution has raised a point of procedure and principle. One of those reasons is not to go into it on something has not brought before the notice and not to go into it with the witness sitting here. If you want to excuse the witness and discuss it further, that's fine. But I'm not going to let Mr. Karnavas, with all due respect, put the evidence in front of the witness and the Chamber on the very point that I've raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's not waste 20 minutes on a detail, on really a ludicrous detail. Based on what Mr. Karnavas said it was just prior to 12.30, just before 12.30 that this was mentioned. It was mentioned that Mr. Izetbegovic came. Is that how Mr. Karnavas said? Did you mention this meeting only this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I mentioned it at about 1.00, as a matter of fact. Between noon and 1.00, early this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Karnavas, you did not have enough time to send e-mails to everybody. Well, proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you could please describe to us this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I was still a member of the War Presidency of Jablanica municipality, and there had been an announcement that Mr. Izetbegovic would be arriving. I, too, was called to the meeting. At the meeting he wanted to see what the political and security-related situation was as well as the economic situation in Jablanica. This was a meeting of the Presidency that included the full component, but there were also some other people such as managers of local companies and businesses, for example, and at one point Mr. Izetbegovic asked the manager of the Jablanica hydroelectric plant, Mr. Muharem Tanovic, the following question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, if you could just wait. I would prefer having the full attention of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Karnavas, I am a bit puzzled for the following reason: On page 53, when you first answered the Prosecution, you said, and I quote: "The gentleman was questioned extensively and extensively by the Prosecution when he gave a 92 bis statement."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So that must be some time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And you know that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Now you say you could only know today at 1.00 that you would bring up this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. Okay. Perhaps it's being lost in translation, and again I appreciate, Judge Trechsel, your intervention here because it does call into question my integrity as I read your question. The 92 bis statement, which you should have as well, was given for the Halilovic case, as I understand. He was not called as a witness. Why wasn't he called? I leave it for the Prosecution to explain. In any event, in that state -- what I'm trying to convey to you is, you don't take a 92 bis statement as extensive as this one without going into the field. If you look at the statement, it is extensive. Now, I don't know whether they asked him all those details. What I do know is that they had access to the gentleman. They questioned the gentleman. Now, whether they questioned him about everything he knew or some of the things that he knew, I don't know, but they knew at the time that he was a member of the Presidency. That's -- that was my point, that they've had access to this gentleman. They've requested him. I don't know whether they had this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I may well be in error, Mr. Karnavas. I'm always prepared to examine and admit it if it's the case. I had thought that you were intimating that that 92 bis statement the question had come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, it hadn't come up. And that's the whole point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Good. Thank --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What happens is these witnesses sometimes say things because they -- you know, their memory has been jogged, and all of a sudden we're put in a position at the very last moment to try to reconcile the situation and this was one instance when it happened so late, you know, we had to be ready to be in court, we want to be here on time. We -- you know, there's only so much I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This shows that it is good sometimes to ask questions and clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This is what happens. I think this is an absolutely felicitous incident, if it's not a bit exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, this 92 bis statement, I know nothing of it. Was it a 92 bis statement for the Prosecution at the time, or was it for the Halilovic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It was taken by the Prosecution. It was taken by the Prosecution, and it was taken actually in French as well. I point that out because I know that this was one of the rare occasions where they had to translate it from French to English. If I may continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To speed up things a little --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if I understood properly, because there was an objection by Mr. Scott, you meant to say that this 92 bis statement having been taken by the Prosecution, it was up to the Prosecution to ask any relevant question, including questions on this meeting with Izetbegovic who allegedly came. So this morning when you talked about this with the witness, you were informed around 1.00 of this; is that right? This is how I understood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Obviously no investigator can be expected to ask every single question. On the other hand, when information does come up, I'm obligated to try and make a record based on the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Just so the record is clear and I don't want to make too much of it at this point, but when an investigator goes into the field, they normally go on a particular case and are seeking the evidence on -- in connection with a particular investigation, not to ask the witness everything he might possibly know about everything. Now, we don't know what the investigator's objective was in conducting this, but to somehow -- for Mr. Karnavas to somehow excuse this by saying the investigator back at that time should have ask all of these questions and then taking us full circle where this started that that somehow relieves him of the obligation to provide notice and the summaries that are required by the Rules is just -- is just -- stretches things way too far. The obligation is on counsel to provide notice. No matter what I know, if my memory and if my knowledge was a lot better than it is, I might know a lot, and I think I do know quite a bit but that nonetheless relieves Mr. Karnavas of absolutely no point of what his obligations are under the Rules and that is to write a summary not matter -- I may know everything. I don't, but maybe I do. That doesn't relief him of his obligation to comply with the Rules, and frankly -- and I'm sure you can hear in it in my voice -- I'm tired of being told every time we object that we should know. It doesn't matter whether I do know, its's his obligation to provide the notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I think you find it hard to understand what an investigator does. A summary is made that was done by Mr. Karnavas. He provides the summary to you. But it so happens later on when he met with the witness there were things that were not in the statement or in the summary that could appear. And you're right in saying that he has to inform you, but he discovered this at 1.00 this afternoon. So materially speaking, he did not have enough time to send you a long letter and explaining to you that during the proofing session that was mentioned. I think everybody's got that. Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I still have a question on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We have had this problem, of course, when the Prosecution presented their evidence, and it has happened that in the morning before Monday afternoon new things came up, and I remember that sometimes at 1.00 or even at a quarter to 2.00 we had information that furthermore during the proofing such-and-such a new question had come up. Wouldn't that have been possible or preferable?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you know, nothing would please me more if I had their staff and -- which I don't have. And of course I've been repeatedly asked by -- specifically by you, Judge Trechsel, to organise the files in a way that they're user-friendly. We're working under extreme circumstances. I don't have the staff. It's easy to say, well, you know, can't -- who's going to do it, okay? It's one of those things. I am got up at 4.00 in the morning. I'm not crying about it but that's the nature of things. I was working from 4.00 in the morning until all the way until I got here and I had 10 minutes to spare. Ms. Tomanovic was assisting us all the way to the very end. Now, if this is a problem, what we could very well do is I won't go into this area until tomorrow. That gives the Prosecution sufficient time. That's good, but what I do get the impression, Judge Trechsel, is somehow, you -- and perhaps others on the bench -- are under the impression that Karnavas just loves thinking up ways how to obstruct the Prosecution's day, and that's not the case. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's not the case that I think like that, Mr. Karnavas. Not at all. I know you have a difficult task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But the last thing I want to do is stand here and make excuses or provide explanations. We're trying. Things fall between the tracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But I think you made a constructive proposal you could have had someone informed in the course of this afternoon and bring new issues tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can do that. I can do that right now. I can move to the next subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, I don't know if it assists, I think it's quite right the comments that have been made The President also, Your Honour, that when issues do arise at the last moment, prior to the testimony of course it can be raised but -- but given that it has come up, I don't think we need to spend so much time on this issue. If my learned friend is prejudiced at all by in new information coming to light certainly on behalf of Mr. Stojic, we wouldn't object after Mr. Karnavas has finished examination-in-chief that some time be given to the Prosecution to the extent that they need that time in order to effectively and properly prepare for cross-examination on that additional point, but that may be the more expedient way to deal with it rather than going in circles at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, just a word or two, and I think it might be helpful in terms of clarifying this issue. In relation to the objection raised by Judge Trechsel, one thing that I do wish to point out is based on my memory at least the Defence never raised any objections in relation to witness summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No. The Chamber does not raise objections, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It appears that something has been misinterpreted. It was a remark by Judge Trechsel that I was talking about, and the explanation on the previous page of the transcript I just wanted to point out that the Defence never raised any objections in relation to new issues that arose in relation to witness summaries during the OTP's case. We merely raised objections when new topics were touched upon that were not actually part and parcel of the witness statements, and we do know that there is a huge difference between summaries and statements and that the Defence is under no obligation to provide witness statements. Therefore, I do believe that Mr. Karnavas at this point in time is right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, one brief response because it makes our points, and I appreciate my good friend Ms. Alaburic pointing it out. There again we come back to the fundamental distinction. The reason that the Defence couldn't have to raise issues so much about the summaries is because we provide them with so much information. We provide them with a 15, 20-page statement of the witness before the witness -- months, years, in advance, years in advance of the witness coming into court. So they're not so much concerned. Let's face it, they're not so much concerned about the summary. They have a statement. The Prosecution does not. We have a summary, sometimes about two paragraphs. That's what we're given. And that's why, Your Honour, and with great respect, that's why we feel so strongly about it, and that's why we'll continue until the last day of trial, as long as the summaries are not deficient, we will continue to raise the issue. That's all we get, Your Honour, and that's why it's so important. That's why we keep raising it. We don't have 20-page statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas. We've been -- we've spent nearly 20 minutes on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And perhaps during the next break if I could give a verbal to the Prosecution as to what the testimony might be before, because it takes some time to type it out and everything. And I can type it out as well for the record, but I can give them a verbal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to move on to another subject, Mr. Zelenika. We'll get back to this tomorrow, okay? So if we go to the next -- the next topic, and I'm going to focus your attention. We're going to be talking about the -- the HVO and the armed forces. If we go to the next document, which is 1D 00969. And this is dated 6 May 1992. Do you have the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you told us earlier to some of my questions as far as, you know the, the -- the armed forces located in Jablanica municipality, and as I understand it this would confirm what you were saying earlier, that the -- that you have Territorial Defence, the Croatian Defence Council, the Green Berets and others participating in the Jablanica Territorial Defence, or in this unified defence system; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge was the HVO at that time participating?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next document 1D 00970. And this is an announcement. It's 6 May 1992, and this talks about a unified defence system being organised, and again we see that it makes reference to the -- the Croatian Defence Council; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note could we have both microphones for the witness switched on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, this announcement, would that have been made available to all the citizens of Jablanica so they would have known the composition of this unified structure?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Well, I can't say all the citizens but most, most at the time. Our system of channeling information was quite good at the time. We had capable TV, and it had been tasked by the War Presidency to keep everyone informed about key issues. The purpose of this statement was forwarded to be read out, and it was several times in the evening hours over the capable TV, and I do believe that most of the citizens knew about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, 1D 024 -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about Green Berets in this document. Everyone knows that the Green Berets are rather on the side of the BiH than the HVO. This announcement is public, 6 May 1992. I suppose that Mr. Izetbegovic and Halilovic, or that is to say, all those who were in the BiH knew that you had at Jablanica a unified force which gathers the Green Berets and the HVO. Am I mistaken or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the unified armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina comprised two equal components, one being the Territorial Defence, the Green Berets, and the Patriotic League, the other -- the other legal and fully legitimate and equal component was the HVO. These two joint components made up the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina under a Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But my question was Mr. Izetbegovic knew about it. He knew, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He most certainly did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we -- if we go on to the next document, 1D 02471. And now this is 21 May 1992, and this is an order and it says: "All available quantities of meat shall be requisitioned from butchers in the territory of Jablanica municipality for the requirements of the Jablanica Territorial Defence units." Now, at this point in time -- that would include Jablanica as well, the Jablanica Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: In the previous document we saw what the components were of the armed forces. This order, however, strays a little from what we saw a moment ago. It says that all the meat that was requisitioned should be made available to members of the Territorial Defence but not the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 02298. And here we see an order that the military staff, the command of the defence forces of Konjic municipality, is obliged to ensure -- it says "unique" in English, "consumption of crude oil and its derivatives for all members of the defence force (TO and HVO) in Konjic municipalities." Can you -- now, first -- and this is signed by a Dr. Rusmir Hadzihusejnovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And were you aware of the situation in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, to a large extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for those of us not familiar with the terrain, how far is Konjic from Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Twenty-three kilometres. The main town, I mean. The municipal territories, the two municipal territories, Konjic and Jablanica, are to a large extent contiguous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in English it says "unique consumption." Could you please look at the document and tell us, does it say unique or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: It says shared or unified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we go to the next document, 1D 01451. This is 29 June 1992. This is a conclusion approving the distribution of foodstuffs to members of the Jablanica police security station based on the same regulation which applied to members of the Jablanica municipality Territorial Defence. And it's signed -- or we see the name of Nijaz Ivkovic. I take it at this point in time Mr. Ivkovic is the president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what's wrong with this particular conclusion, very quickly, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: This is yet another example of discrimination against the HVO. The HVO is here not being treated as an equal component in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They only deal here with the TO stations -- with the TO and the public security stations, but the HVO seems to be left out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 01543. This is a decision now this is 20 July and it says here "To remain the Territorial Defence as the staff of the Jablanica municipality OS armed forces." Now, is it a fact that after this date the Territorial Defence was renamed to Jablanica Municipality Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: In essence the decision has a purely terminological meaning. We now no longer spoke of the Green Berets, the Patriotic League and the TO. Rather, the new name encompassing all these now was the Armed Forces of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But that did not encompass the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Well, if you go through this decision, one would say not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. 1D 00344. This is 13 November 1992, and here we do see that the restaurant and kitchen, and it's named in here, is -- "... shall be requisitioned to provide quarters for 50 members of the Jablanica HVO." What is this about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. This is about requisitioning a part of that building owned by a socially owned business. They were into catering, and this was to be used by the HVO for HVO purposes, but this wasn't as big as a barracks, for example, or anything, not big enough to put up the soldiers. That's where they ate, where they took their meals, about 50 of them, because that's how big it was. It was no bigger than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. If we look again on the next document, 1D 01462. This is now 19 January, 1993. We're moving in time. And this is an order limiting the sale of oil and oil derivatives. And if we look at Article I, it says: "The sale of oil and oil derivatives by the Jablanica petrol station is hereby limited except for the quantities at the disposal of the Jablanica HVO," and then it goes on. Can you confirm to us that indeed the HVO at this particular point in time was receiving oil and oil derivatives per this order of the Presidency of the Jablanica municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The purpose of this decision primarily was to rationalise on the use of oil and oil derivatives given the fact that the HVO got its petrol from the petrol station, they were actually renting the petrol station for that purpose. This restriction in no way applied to the HVO but, rather, to the component that belonged to the BH armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at 1D 01463. Again -- now we are into January 22, 1993, and this is a conclusion by the Presidency in Jablanica on approving the agreement on the conditions and manner of sale and distribution of fuel by the Energopetrol station in Jablanica, and it makes reference to the Jablanica Municipal Assembly and the Jablanica HVO. Are we speaking of the Jablanica HVO, the -- the armed component or the civilian component? And I'm told ...

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: We're talking here about the civilian component of the HVO. An agreement was reached with them, a conditional one for them to supply and sell fuel at the petrol station in Jablanica. This is a conclusion, but there's another document which is the full scale -- or, rather, detailed agreement on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If you could go back to the previous document, 1D 01462 and look at page 2 of that agreement. Tell me -- tell us whether you're referring to this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So we have to look at these two documents together?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So we have to look at these two documents together; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, as a whole, together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We'll move on to another segment. And this is a sort of a short topic. This deals with UNHCR. And if we look at 1D 01449. This is 1 May 1992. You've already told us that this is a unified armed forces in the sense that HVO is -- is fully recognised. So now going back to May 1, 1992, with this document, 1D 01449, we see that there's a decision by Sefer Hamdo where he says to give 2.500 meals given as aid by the UN High Commissariat to the Jablanica Territorial Defence, to staff. My first question is these meals that were given by the UN, were they intended for military purposes or civilian purposes?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The meals provided by UNHCR were meals for military purposes in the case at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were they for military or for civilian? That's what I'm asking, not where they actually went to.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Understandably the UNHCR looked after civilians, so it was for civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And in looking at this decision, is -- when it says the Jablanica Territorial Defence, would that include also the HVO getting their 20 per cent of the 2.500 meals, which by my math it's about 500.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No. This decision does not imply that the HVO would be getting their 20 per cent cut over a total of 2.500. This decision is actually not in keeping with the documents that we were looking at a while ago about there being two equally recognised components of the defence plan. Based on this decision the HVO would be getting nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, perhaps we can go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Back in open session. We're going to have a 20-minute break, and we'll resume at 6.10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have 50 minutes left before the end of the day. Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And then perhaps we can have two or three minutes prior to the end of the day where I do want to go on record and give a -- give the Trial Chamber an indication of that material, that information, in the presence of the Prosecution so you can have that. It's an offer of proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go on to the next document of 1D 00780. This is the next chapter, sir. This deals with the issue of curfew. And it's not part of tu quoque. It is to indicate what is happening in the Jablanica municipality at the time. Now, we see this is 10 April 1992, and we see that a curfew is being imposed. If you could tell us why was it necessary to impose a curfew in Jablanica as early as 10 April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: At this time a curfew was introduced because it was necessary to introduce it due to the fact that there was a large number of displaced persons in Jablanica, a large number of refugees, mainly local population. Those were the reason. And according to the reports of the police, there was a large -- there was a high incidence of offences and violations against law and order, and that was the reason why it was necessary to introduce a curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. And we'll just look at one other document, and there will be others for the Trial Chamber by way of motion. 1D 00990. Here we have a decision on the introduction of a curfew, and this is 28 May 1992. And I take it that your answer would be the same with this decision as it was with the one that you've just told us about; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. While we're on the issue of -- sort of issues of controlling, were there -- were there check-points placed at the city entrance and exit?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Correct. Check-points had already been set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who was manning those check-points?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: They were manned by the reserve force of the police, mixed crews of the members of Muslim armed forces and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We're going to go on to the next chapter, and this deals with roads. We did such a little bit on this. You spoke about the Road of Salvation or to Salvation. If we look at 1D 00953. This is 20 April 1992. And here we have a decision to send a request to the Crisis Staff for the municipality of Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, and Bugojno to give to Jablanica municipality some machinery and five to six tons of fuel so that urgent and necessary interventions of the Jablanica-Risovac road may be carried out. First let me ask you, are you familiar with this stretch of the road, Jablanica-Risovac?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. That's the regional road R-419, the Salvation Road that we had mentioned when discussing the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And again -- well, why was it necessary to contact the municipalities of Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, and Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Because at that time Jablanica had a problem with fuel, and we thought -- we knew, rather, that fuel was available in the municipalities you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And this particular road, the Jablanica-Risovac, where would it go? If you could kind of help us out here.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: It led to the west of the municipality centre. Jablanica is an hub of roads from Sarajevo, from the direction of Banja Luka. Those roads meet at Jablanica. And since it was impossible to go towards Mostar, the only way to go was Doljani, Posusje, Split. That's about 60 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And to your knowledge were any refugees going to Split from Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: They were going almost every day. I know that. And it was necessary to keep that road usable, open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what period of are we speaking of when they were going to Split?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: So we are now discussing the first part of 1992, and they kept going until mid-1992 in larger numbers that were later reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You say first part of 1992. Now, what months are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: According to this document, we are now in April. They kept going until mid-April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Where were they coming from? What parts of the country were they coming from?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Refugees came to Jablanica mainly from the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the areas of Foca, Rudo, Gorazde, and some from Eastern Herzegovina, Gacko, Nevesinje, and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So when we speak of refugees, we're actually speaking of displaced persons. These are residents or citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. Those were residence of one part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And they're passing through from what I understand from Jablanica and they're going now to the Republic of Croatia, another country, neighbouring country; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, were they being forced to go to Croatia by Jablanica municipality? Were they being kicked out?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No. We organised it at their request. Many of them actually insisted to have passage towards Split. On many occasions we provided the buses for their transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll go on to the next document, 1D 00957. Here we have April 25, 1992, and we see that "the Jablanica Territorial Defence Staff is ordered to ensure the road to Posusje -- that the road to Posusje is permanently opened." Now, why was that necessary?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: This order confirms what we will discussed on the previous document, the importance of that road and the need to keep it open so that the refugees coming from northern areas of Bosnia would be able to go towards Split and on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The next document is 1D 00972, and here we see an order, and this is -- we see a Mostar state-owned company is ordered to provide a bus with 25 seats to transport workers engaged on the construction of the Sovici-Risovac-Posusje road from Jablanica to Risovac and back and my question now is how is it that the Jablanica municipality Crisis Staff is ordering a construction company or a state-owned company which is from Mostar? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Well, at that time these -- the vehicles happened to be in Jablanica. So the Crisis Staff thought that all the resources that happened to be in the territory of the municipality could be used for what they believed to be a priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So in other words they were confiscating it and using it.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Even though it belonged to perhaps another municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00992. Here this is decision to begin the construction of the Jablanica-Posusje-Sovici section. And we see this is R-419. This is the same road I take it that we've been talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, that is the same road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And finally if we look at the next document, 1D 0450. This has to do with the repair of bridges on Jablanica-Mostar main road. This is 23 June 1992. What was it necessary to repair bridges? What was the problem?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The bridges on this section Jablanica-Mostar had been blown up and destroyed, and the interventions we see referred to here were not aimed at completely restoring the bridges, nor was it possible. The purpose was to enable them to be used for pedestrian traffic or perhaps even passenger vehicles but not freight vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That concludes that section, but let me ask one question. Did the HVO military component or the HVO civilian component in any way try to obstruct the building of this road or the repair of the bridges?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No, on the contrary. The HVO took an active part with all its resources, both technical and manpower.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We're going to go on to the same segment, and this deals with some issues on the economy, loosely phrased, so nobody should hold me to it or hold it against me for not having a more comprehensive title. 1D 00937 -- 973, 973. This is 8 May 1992, and this is an order, and we can see that it talks about instructing all companies, the SDK, that's the Public Auditing Service, the Sarajevo commercial bank branches and the post offices that they're to place their materiel and technical equipment resources and money at the disposal of the Jablanica municipal Crisis Staff. Can you tell us, please, why was this necessary? What does this order exactly mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: This order had a purpose of placing cash from the SDK, the bank or other publicly owned enterprises to the Crisis Staff so that they could fund the logistical needs of the municipality of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we've heard testimony before, and we'll hear it again -- or we'll hear testimony again, I should say, concerning this Public Auditing Service, the SDK as it was known back then. Could you please tell us whether the Public Auditing Service for Jablanica, whether it was tied into the greater network throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, there's nothing about the SDK or the economy. There's nothing whatsoever in the summary about this, so we would object to evidence on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are documents that again are rather clear on their face. There is nothing in the summary again when we go to the next document that has Jugo dinars, German marks and Croatian dinars. Now, let's put it into context. We've had testimony regarding the Public Auditing Service, and this gentleman was there. I'm discussing this particular order. These documents were disclosed to the Prosecution, and I see absolutely no issue with this. I mean, I -- and also, as it was pointed out to me, and I'm very grateful to my colleagues that I failed to mention, that if there's any prejudice suffered or being suffered or to be suffered by the Prosecution as a result of this -- of this document or other documents or testimony coming from the witness, then perhaps after my direct examination, you could determine to what extent any -- if any he was prejudiced and fight the appropriate remedy such as, because you must take the least restrictive measure, give him an opportunity to prepare. But this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not the remedy. As Judge Trechsel has correctly pointed out, and it's quite relevant now again, id what Mr. Karnavas wants to do is just simply read 65 ter (G) out of the rules. Let's just take the rule book and tear those out and say they don't apply to me. And say the rules don't apply to me. Is that the Chamber's ruling? Because it's not in the summary, and there is no reason for all this. Mr. Scott should it's not in the summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's he like four sentences. It's either in the summary or it's not, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The gentleman was provided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, please -- allow me please first to make this final comment, and I'll abide whatever decision you make on 31st of March, 2008 we provided detailed list of documents we intended it use with -- with the -- with our witnesses. Now, it is incumbent upon the Prosecution to read those documents. They should know what is in those documents. Jablanica municipality is in the indictment, after all. They also had the gentleman's background, and just by looking at the gentleman's summary they would have known that we were discussing issues related to Jablanica municipality. Now, what is the purpose of -- if I may, Judge Trechsel, make my record, and I would appreciate being heard and then I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have not much new argument, Mr. Karnavas, the same all over again. And I refer you to Rule 65 ter (G)(i)(b) and what you say is different. It is not what the Rules say. It's as simple as that. The Rules say you must warn about the facts. You must give a summary of the facts the witness will speak about, and you want to escape that. You simply do not want to accept it. I think that is not -- it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I beg to differ with you, Judge Trechsel. Nobody's trying to escape anything. But I'll move on. I'm go on. If the SDK upsets the Prosecution and it upsets you, and you feel that somehow we didn't disclose this material, we'll move on. Let me just ask one question since we are on this particular document -- since we are on this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, please move on to something else, but my colleague is absolutely right. The Rules say that you have to sum up the facts to which the -- each and every witness is going to testify. So that's the Rule. This is not something said by the Judges. It is in the Rules. Therefore, if the Prosecutor sees there is one fact mentioned by you that is note in the summary each time he will be on his feet to tell you have not complied with your obligation. Therefore, in the future do list all the facts in your summaries. That will be, you know, gaining time, saving time for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you in Jablanica at this particular time, 8 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Look at the next document, 1D 00783. And here we have a decision on fuel prices, and it lists dinars, German marks, Croatian dinars. With respect to the first list of dinars, are they -- where are they from?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection exactly the same. Apparently Mr. Karnavas didn't hear the objection or the ruling. Economy, currency, none of that is in the summary, and he's just proceeding on, and I thought the Court made it quite clear. I thought Judge Trechsel and the President made it quite clear these were outside the scope of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can solve this problem. We can send this gentleman back at this point to his hotel. I can prepare another summary, and we can start again on Wednesday. It's as simple as that. But I find it rather curious that here's somebody who was the president of the Executive Council. Now he's talking about the situation in Jablanica and members -- some members of the trial bench simply do not find this to be information that is necessary or relevant to the case, and the Defence is being accused of not having complied with the Rules. By virtue of his position, he is able to talk about what is happening in Jablanica, and I don't see how the Prosecution is being prejudiced. That's the real issue. How are they being prejudiced by this? But since we have Judge Trechsel shaking his head with virtually everything I say, I suggest, Mr. President, that at this point -- at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- at the end of the day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, faced with this specific problem the Trial Chamber is trying to find a practical solution, which is for you to continue with the examination-in-chief based on the points expressly mentioned in your summary. With regard to the ones that are not in the summary, do disclose to the Prosecution tonight at the latest the points that were not in the summary but are to be found in the documents or in the document that you have the list of exhibits so that on -- documents, so that Mr. Scott knows tomorrow what your topics will be, and you'll have the whole night to prepare for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I must confess that I don't have my summary in front of me, and based on that -- I mean, this is one of those rare occasions where we didn't bring it. It wasn't intentional like some may assume. I just don't have my summary here, and I assume that I'm going to be asked to justify on every single document even though it's been disclosed as of the 31st of March to the Prosecution concerning these witnesses. But I don't have my summary, and therefore I suggest that we adjourn for the day. I can then prepare a more detailed summary for the Prosecution and have it to them hopefully by 9.00, no later than 9.00, perhaps even earlier. So that would be my suggestion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, not to belabour the matter, but if I get a list of these issues at midnight tonight I do not have time to prepare for cross-examination tomorrow. What the Rules require is that they be provided on the 31st of March, 2008. Well, I hear laughter coming from the other side. That's completely inappropriate. That's what the Rules require, it's what the Chamber ordered. Your Scheduling Order said that this information would be provided to the Prosecution on the 31st of March, 2008, not at midnight the night before cross-examination, and I will not conduct a cross-examination on that basis. I have to have -- I have every right to prepare. So if Mr. Karnavas is in violation of the Rules, which he is, more than six months late, more than six months late, I will not have that date to the prejudice of the Prosecution to prepare. It's his violation, not mine. Do not penalize the Prosecution for the violations of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, once again I can just suggest that Your Honours' ruling stands. The information can be provided, and if after receiving the information at the end of examination-in-chief my learned friend still things that more time is needed, at that point an application for additional time can be made. It's a matter that can be dealt with I think to ensure that the Prosecution is not prejudiced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The analysis is fundamentally flawed, Your Honour the rules do not require --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott. I think that's a fair proposal. You don't necessarily have to start tomorrow, but you can do it later. We know that the Rules have not really been complied with, but we somehow have to get through this trial. We still hope that the compliance will eventually improve with 65 ter, but I do not entirely discard the reference to possible prejudice. Anyway, there is already in the air possibility that the witness might be called back at a later stage in connection with the -- with the expert opinion, and I think somehow we must find ways that prevent this from totally collapsing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With due respect, Your Honour, the way to deal with it is to enforce the Rules, and if the Chamber -- with the greatest of respect and with great respect, Judge Mindua my great respect to you, Judge Prandler my great respect, Mr. President my great respect, Judge Trechsel my great respect. If the Chamber would enforce the Rules once and for all and make it very clear that this would be solved, but instead this happens to the prejudice of the Prosecution. The Rules require but we'll excuse it this time and the next time and the next time, and it's the always the Prosecution that is the loser in these -- Rule 65 ter (G) says nothing about prejudice. The obligation stands on Defence counsel and says nothing about -- except where it doesn't prejudice the Prosecution. The way -- with the greatest of respect -- the way for the Chamber to deal with this issue is to make its ruling on the summaries once and for all, make it very clear and make the Defence comply. Then we won't have these problems because we'll have -- hopefully we'll have compliance not tomorrow or not so the Prosecution has to run in at the last minute, but we'll have compliance for the rest of the trial if the Chamber enforces the Rules now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, just one additional point. Of course in drafting the Rules, the Judges of this Tribunal eschewed the possibility of technical rules of evidence, and there is of course a whole raft of possibilities between a breach, a mere breach, and a substantial breach, and in assessing the remedy, the remedy for a breach Your Honours would have reference and recourse of course to Rule 89 to decide on the Rules -- the best favor in a fair determination the master. I understand it's quite palpable my learned friend is upset, and I'm not trying to condone I'm not taking a partisan position here, but from the way I think the Trial Chamber's ruling must be understood, it's been specifically tailored to avoid any possibility of prejudice to the Prosecution, because what could the prejudice be? The prejudice would -- the prejudice of course would be if they are taken by surprise and are being compelled to cross-examine information of a nature which they could not anticipate and couldn't properly address and prepare for. Your Honours' ruling in my respectful submission focuses on that. My learned friend can provide a more detailed information. My learned friend Mr. Scott can see it, and if at the time of reading it it is of nature that requires a more sophisticated approach, requires more time there's going to be no objection from this Defence team if that time is granted to the Prosecution, so I think matters can be kept rather -- rather calm and matters can be dealt with in an unremarkable manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it wasn't my intention previously to use up any time, but I think matters have now gone too far and we should have the positions of the other Defence teams. I wish to pick up where Mr. Khan left off. I fully agree with him. However, and I think this applies to every Rule as it does to Rule 64, we must first have a fair interpretation. In itself the Rule means nothing. It is not before you've placed it in the context of the overall trial that we can grasp its full meaning. What is its meaning? I think that's visible from the practice. We must provide summaries before a witness appears and the point -- and this is to avoid surprise, to avoid any traps being laid by one party for the other. Nobody can be allowed to bring a witness without the other party knowing exactly what the witness will be testifying about. Of course there are matters of detail involved, but we must look at any specific situation as it arises. How could the OTP possibly have been surprised if, (a) in addition to the summary provided by Mr. Karnavas, (b)it received a list of documents and in that list were also the documents that the Prosecutor now claims is not in the summary? Does this mean that we actually have to recount documents in our summaries? The indictment was raised five or six years ago. They know the case. The OTP know the facts or perhaps they have not been acting conscientiously, or perhaps they at the time raised their indictment without knowing the facts. When I or Mr. Karnavas give the Prosecution a list of documents and what each witness will be questioned about, then they must understand. This is crystal clear. Money, currency. Even an infant would know what this is about. We cannot interpret this provision verbatim. Summary and then you need to list all the facts that you will be asking a witness about. This has to be a more general type of information. This is a summary, also a list of documents. When talking about this witness this is also something else his 92 bis statement the one that the witness provided to them. Therefore the OTP know full well what this witness might or might not be talking about. Hence I believe that the OTP's claim that it has been ambushed or prejudiced has nothing to it that is true. Let's not be naive about this. Let's not have the Rule read out verbatim as it reads with no context, with no possibility of contextual or circumstantial interpretation. This is something that simply doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the transcript, page 98, line 24, Mr. Kovacic, you don't want to speak about Rule 64. You mean 65 ter, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Now, we have devoted perhaps one hour on these problems, on these issues. I wanted to use this hour to ask questions which would have been very interesting and which I cannot ask because we have a procedural problem. And I say it's a pity both for the Prosecution and the Defence. This being said, Mr. Karnavas is going to address the -- to send the list of items which is not in the summary on which he intends to ask questions from the witness on the remaining documents. And then this is my personal point of view: This question of the possible prejudice for the Prosecution, yes, he's right, but the question is to know may there be a prejudice. The Defence could also in another situation talk about the prejudice. I wonder where is the prejudice. The documents that have been contested up to now have concerned dinars, for instance, documents 783 on the price of petrol, or 788, diesel. I don't know what the prejudice can be for a person who sees that the 98 is 1.40 Deutschmark. So one should be in a position when one knows the case, and it's been for years that one should be knowing the case that this trial has begun. One shouldn't be surprised by this document. Perhaps for certain people it's a prejudice. For me it's not because I discovered the document at the last minute. So the Chamber might also say there is a problem. One discovers documents. So we could say in the future each time the Defence prepares a file, I need at least a fortnight to prepare myself. If not, I will suffer prejudice, and justice will suffer prejudice with that. The trial will go on for years, at least 20 years. So everybody has to do their best, and Defence must in the future do its best to present the facts on which -- on D1 and D2 in order to avoid to lose time because all the time that is lost, more than 20 per cent devoted to procedural matters could have been used to go to substantive matters, substantive issue, it would have been more interesting for everybody. So, Mr. Karnavas, make an effort to review all this in order to get to Mr. Scott as soon as the list in question, and therefore you might -- you may continue your examination. Do you want to add something, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, just briefly, Your Honour. We could send the witness out at this point, and I could spend the next ten minutes in -- giving a verbal account as far as what I'm going to cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes. All right. So, Witness, the hearing will resume tomorrow, tomorrow morning at 9.00. Now you're going to leave -- now you're going to leave courtroom, and we'll see you again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you have used up nearly two hours now so you still have two hours and two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope. I really hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me go back to the one issue that was into the in -- that we learned today. That goes to the Izetbegovic meeting. Based on what the witness indicated to us, he was invited to this meeting. It wasn't known at the time I guess it had escaped everyone's attention that he was the only non-Muslim there. At that point in time when the meeting took place Mr. Izetbegovic concreting asked the director of the hydroelectric plant whether they could cut off the electricity to this area called Herceg-Bosna at which point in time the director said yes that could be done and Izetbegovic said that's good. That was all that we learned on that. Now, to go on to the next -- to the segments that we had planned out based on the documents that we had presented to the Court and to the Prosecution for this particular witness, the economy, all these documents, I think you've said it, Mr. President. Basically they all reflect the fact that you have the use of the German mark, also the Croatian dinar. Why is that important? It's important because of this argument of Croatisation. We see that Croatian dinars are being used in official documents, and that was to show that at that point in time people were using whatever was available to them under the circumstances. With respect to the SDK, the Public Auditing Service, it's well known that Jablanica was connected as every other municipality and every, you know, locality to the central system which wasn't functioning and that we heard already from Mr. Primorac. So that deals with that segment. The next segment deals with movements and mobilisation. That's what we called or that's what I called it. Go you look at these documents these are all official documents that we got from the municipality, they're rather very plain on their face. They're talking -- these are steps that were taken by the municipality at the time. It has nothing to do with tu quoque. What it has to do is to show that under these extraordinary circumstances miraculously or serendipitously all these municipalities are acting more or less in the same fashion. Why? Because those were necessary measures to take under the circumstances. Nothing nefarious about that. And we see even the very last document that was included, we have an order for mobilisation and what was interesting was here is Dr. Cibo, a medical doctor, who is mobilising from the age of 15 up to the age of 65, and I only pointed that out because as I recall two and a half years ago the issue was the age of mobilization. We see 18, sometimes 17, sometimes 16, and here we have a document on 15. There are no mysteries to this particular segment. They're all, if you read them, they very plainly talk about what was happening at the time. Then we go on to this issue dealing with the civilian authorities, that is the War Presidency and the executive the documents are laid out in a chronological order again to give the Trial Chamber a flavour as to how things unfold starting with the gentleman's position that he held and certain decisions that were issued. They're rather plain on their face. At some point we get to the issue of Cibo. He's been here -- he's been mentioned on numerous occasions, and, yes, we will be asking about Cibo's appointment and he will state that Cibo's appointment was unconstitutional at the time. He was there as the war president for Konjic, Jablanica, and I believe Prozor as well. And this -- this also I should go and I'm grateful to my colleague Ms. Tomanovic. This testimony came in from Idrizovic. If you may recall, this gentleman talked about -- about Jablanica, and of course we are at the stage where we are entitled to rebut testimony by the Prosecution. So all of these documents -- or not all but some of these documents go to address if not rebut some of the information that was brought in by witness Idrizovic. And of course what we're going to show is that with the coming of Cibo the events deteriorate. My -- the witness is in forced labour. At some point he's at a camp. And of course the Executive Council becomes purely Muslim at that stage. So that's -- and also we're going to be talking about the issue of Okruzi, which is the districts. That issue has already come up, its constitutionality and how it worked. The next segment is -- deals with mobilisation of -- of resources. Now, there are lots of documents. We had over 20 or 30 documents at one point. Some we will address through motion, but what we wanted to show that again when Dr. Cibo comes in and we do -- we do submit that this -- this individual is rather unique in his approach. We see that he begins to commandeer the first two documents, the commandeering, wood, and flower stuff, but it's only from Croats. That's what the witness will say, that while they were commandeering and while they were expropriating, it was only from the Croats and not from the Muslims from Jablanica, again to show the situation there. And why is all of this somewhat important? Because it goes -- it goes to our overall concept and theory which was well understood by the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina that in these times of need, they needed to organise themselves, and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, especially in Jablanica, was for that very same purpose, to organise themselves so that -- as an association, as group. They could protect themselves without necessarily trying to do anything nefarious as has been outlined by the Prosecution. So -- and if you look at the other documents, they're very innocuous in that there's nothing special. The last document for instance 1D 01483. It shows here that Dr. Cibo is now commandeering the pharmacy and the pharmaceuticals of the Caritas, Croatian Catholic charity, and he's putting it at the disposal of the Jablanica town pharmacy for "better use" under him. And so -- now, again if we look at these documents, you will see that they're rather -- they're not very complicated. They're one-page documents. They have been provided. The next issue deals with the camps. Now, certainly the Prosecution should know all about this issue because the gentleman was -- was not only taken to a camp but he was tortured. He had a terrible experience, and of course the first document is this Jablanica war hospital. This is where he went and they refused to examine him because of his particular situation. That's when he was put under slave labour as he put it. Then we have lists of -- of Croats who were in the Museum in Jablanica. This testimony came out during the Prosecution's case. So again this is not a mystery. This was testified to as well by Mr. Idrizovic. So again this is evidence that goes to counter the Prosecution's case, much of which I find it very difficult to believe that the Prosecution is unaware of or is surprised by. The documents are rather self-evident. One of the things that might be interesting in this packet which I find kind of interesting is appointment by Sefer Halilovic. He appoints Cibo, who is the Presidency, he's the president of the Presidency, now he appoints him to a military position and then later on we see Dr. Cibo issuing operational orders. That would be 1D 03039. So -- and then there was a chronology which was prepared by -- by the gentleman, and I assume they would know about this chronology because for years the gentleman worked for the office of the -- the Office of the Prosecutor investigators. He worked with them for several years. They relied on him to gather information for the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, Office of the Prosecution. And then finally the last is his certificate of release from the camp. And finally there is one chapter which we don't know whether we will have time to get to, and that deals with the issue of refugees, and again if you look at them, that's merely to demonstrate how the -- the refugees were coming and how they were going, and again we heard some testimony that refugees went straight to Croatia. Again, that was their wish. That's how they ended up there. Albeit this is the timing of 1992, but again it goes to that. In addition to this, he will talk about how the abandoned -- how the refugees were accommodated in Jablanica at one point where the Croats were forced to -- to accommodate large members of families -- large family -- families in their own apartments to the point that some of them ultimately either had to leave or it became rather difficult for them to be in that situation and left on their own. This particular gentleman was housing nine. He will recount one time when Croats were brought to the Museum and the little boy from the family came back and said, "Mama, I just went down and tried to beat up some Ustasha." And the mother kind of told him to hush because after all he was saying this in the presence of the witness in the witness's own house. So this is essentially his testimony. Why is this relevant? Again it goes to this whole notion that as of 1991 the Croatian Community -- there was this joint criminal enterprise, and what the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was all about and how it fits into this enterprise and anybody who participated in it was a member of this joint criminal enterprise, the notion that there was this territory, that they're trying to re-establish the Banovina Hrvatska, that they actually through their own one witness indicated Idrizovic. That they tried to take over the civilian authorities where, in fact, we see nothing of the sort happened. They pitched an idea. It was rejected. That was it. That is in essence the testimony of the gentleman, and what I will do tonight pursuant to your -- to your instructions, I will sit down and I will try to put it in writing and -- and frankly let me say again with all due candour when I came here today, now, maybe I misread the situation, but I believed in my heart-of-hearts that I had fully complied with my obligations as far as the summaries go. Now, some may disagree. I truly believed that the Prosecution, based on their representation, that I didn't need to supplement any more, were aware I was going to go into these sorts of subjects because that's what would be expected in late of the gentleman's background. I truly apologise to the Prosecution if I've caused them any grief. I will certainly endeavour in the future to do better. I will go back even to next -- the next witness who they've asked not to supplement. I will see if I can supplement it some more so that we don't have this recurrence, and I apologise to the Bench for wasting more procedural time. It certainly wasn't intended but I can assure you we're doing our best to become as we possibly can be so that we can provide the evidence that you need in order to make a fair determination in this case and I thank you very much for granting me this time. Thank you and good night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we're going to stop because now we've gone beyond the time. You spoke of next witness. I'm looking at the list of documents for the next witness. We've got 373 exhibits. Experience shows that in six hours, one may admit 90 -- 80 exhibits. So you will have to sort out your exhibits, because there is a great number of these exhibits which you'll have to sort out since you will not be in a position to tender them. You will only be able to tender about 80 to a hundred. Here you've got 373, which will cause a problem. Therefore, I'll give Mr. Scott which he is entitled to receive and act on the statement you've made and then things will go much better, because I just said I prefer to go to the bottom of things, the substance, rather than to spend 20 per cent of our time in procedural matters because the judgement will be on the substance and not on procedure. So good evening and see you tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of October, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 25
